This dimension represents the maximum shell length recorded for Cerastoderma glaucum, a value observed in older individuals inhabiting stable, low-intertidal zones with consistent salinity. The transition from a free-swimming planktonic larva to a benthic post-metamorphic juvenile is a critical period in the life cycle. During this phase, larval metamorphosis and subsequent settlement onto a suitable substrate are prerequisites for successful recruitment. The time since birth at metamorphosis has been documented as 11 days since birth  when water temperatures are maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a thermal condition that accelerates the development of the veliger larva through the pediveliger stage. This relatively brief pelagic duration is typical for many cardid bivalves inhabiting shallow, seasonally warm coastal lagoons, where rapid settlement may reduce the risk of advection into unfavorable environments.

Following successful metamorphosis and recruitment to the benthos, the newly settled spat undergo a period of rapid body growth. At a shell length of 15 millimeters, the wet weight of an individual has been recorded at 0.17 grams . This allometric relationship between shell dimension and tissue mass provides a useful metric for assessing body condition in field populations. The initial mass at the start of independent life is exceedingly small; based on the diameter of the fertilised ovum, the wet weight at birth from an embryonated egg is calculated to be 0.00000022 grams [Wwb = 0.00000022 grams]. This minute size reflects the lecithotrophic, yolk-dependent larval strategy, where the embryo relies entirely on internal reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. Following eclosion from the egg capsule, the trochophore larva rapidly develops into a planktotrophic veliger that feeds on phytoplankton using cilia-driven feeding currents. The duration of this yolk-sac stage is remarkably short; the age at birth is approximately 3 days [ab = approximately 3 days] at a temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C].

Within the family Cardiidae, the reproductive output of Cerastoderma glaucum is comparable to that of the common cockle Cerastoderma edule. At a stable water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the lifespan of the Lagoon cockle has been estimated at approximately 1,825 days [am = approximately 1,825 days]. The process of gamete fusion following broadcast spawning is external, with syngamy occurring in the water column after sperm transfer. The resulting zygote quickly develops into a yolk-laden egg that contains sufficient nutrients to support the embryo through the initial cleavage stages. Female Cerastoderma glaucum can release eggs during peak spawning events at a rate that reflects the maximum reproductive capacity typical of cardid bivalves in temperate coastal lagoons.

The disparity in body size between the larval and adult stages is immense, reflecting a life history strategy centered on rapid growth and high fecundity. The species reaches a maximum shell length of 5 centimeters [Li = 5 centimeters] only after several years of sustained feeding and shell deposition. The time required to reach this exotrophic transition is tightly linked to temperature; the age at birth of approximately 3 days [ab = approximately 3 days] at 11 °C [T = 11 °C] indicates a rapid early development relative to many other marine bivalves. This accelerated embryogenesis allows the larvae to exploit ephemeral phytoplankton blooms, which are common in the shallow, productive lagoons that the species inhabits.

Field surveys of Cerastoderma glaucum populations indicate that the period between larval settlement and the attainment of reproductive maturity spans several months. A total length at puberty of 0.96 cm [Lp = 0.96 cm] serves as a key demographic threshold used in population models to predict the onset of gametogenesis. Individuals that have not yet reached this size remain as immature post-metamorphic juveniles, diverting all available resources toward body growth rather than gonadal development. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species, approximately 1,825 days [am = approximately 1,825 days], is often shortened by natural mortality factors such as predation by shorebirds, crab predation, and winter ice scour at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. For those that survive, the final body size of 5 centimeters [Li = 5 centimeters] is a robust indicator of a reproductively active adult with a well-developed gonad. The initial planktonic stage, lasting just 11 days from birth  to metamorphosis at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], is remarkably brief for a species that can ultimately persist for several years, illustrating a life history that prioritizes rapid colonization of suitable substrates followed by a longer, stable adult phase focused on repeated spawning events.
